content_units: Vancouver Tenancy Intake Snapshot

This intake checklist is for a   British Columbia residential tenancy   in   Vancouver   based on the facts provided: a fixed-term lease from   2025-09-01 to 2026-08-31  , a   half-month security deposit  , and a landlord’s written notice on   2026-06-15   claiming a   12% rent increase effective 2026-08-01  .

On those facts alone, the main screening issues are likely the   validity and timing of the rent increase  , whether the   correct BC notice form   was used, and what happens at the   end of the fixed term  .
BC Tenancy Verification Checklist
Item   What to verify   Why it matters   Intake note

Lease term   Exact start/end dates and whether the agreement says it continues month-to-month after the term   End-of-term rights often depend on lease wording and BC tenancy rules   Confirm signed lease matches 2025-09-01 to 2026-08-31

Rent amount   Current monthly rent, due date, and whether any utilities/parking/storage are included   Needed to calculate any claimed increase and total exposure   Record current lawful rent precisely

Deposit   Exact deposit paid, payment date, and whether any pet deposit was also charged   BC limits deposits and handling rules matter at move-out   Half-month security deposit appears typical; verify receipt

Rent increase notice   Whether notice was on the proper BC form, served correctly, and gave enough notice   A rent increase can be invalid even if given in writing   Notice dated 2026-06-15 for 2026-08-01 needs close review
Increase amount   Whether 12% exceeds the permitted annual increase unless specially approved   Over-limit increases are commonly disputed   No renovation basis is identified in your facts

Reason for increase   Whether landlord claims capital expenditures, new services, or any RTB authorization   The reason affects whether the increase may be lawful   Facts suggest no major renovations planned

Fixed-term ending   Whether landlord is claiming the tenancy ends automatically on 2026-08-31   In BC, fixed terms do not always simply end unless specific legal conditions apply   Check any move-out clause carefully
Documents to Gather Before Legal Advice
-   Signed tenancy agreement   and any renewals, addenda, house rules, or amendments.
-   Rent increase notice   exactly as received, including envelope, email headers, text message screenshots, or service details.
-   Proof of current rent  :
- rent receipts
- e-transfer confirmations
- bank statements
- ledger or payment history
-   Proof of deposit payment   and any receipt issued by the landlord.
-   All communications with the landlord   about rent, renewal, move-out, or lease end:
- emails
- texts
- letters
- notices posted on the door
-   Move-in condition inspection report   and photos/videos from move-in.
-   Any notices about ending tenancy  , renovations, personal use, sale of unit, or proposed new lease.
-   Copy of the written notice dated 2026-06-15   showing the proposed   12% increase starting 2026-08-01  .
-   Current and prior rent amounts   so the exact dollar increase can be calculated.
-   Identification of the landlord entity  :
- individual owner
- property manager
- company name
- service address
-   Proof of service details   if known:
- when the tenant actually received the notice
- how it was delivered
- who delivered it
Questions the Tenant Should Ask the Landlord
- What is the   current monthly rent   and what exact   new monthly rent   is being demanded?
- Was the increase served using the   official BC rent increase form  ?
- How was the notice delivered, and on what date does the landlord say it was   received  ?
- Why is the landlord seeking a   12% increase  ?
- Has the landlord obtained   Residential Tenancy Branch approval   for an amount above the standard annual increase, if required?
- Is the landlord saying the tenant must sign a   new fixed-term lease   to stay?
- Does the landlord believe the tenancy   ends automatically on 2026-08-31  , and if so, on what basis?
- Is the landlord planning any change in included services, parking, storage, or utilities that they say justifies the increase?
- Are there any other notices coming, such as for   landlord use  ,   sale  , or   renovations  ?
- Will the landlord provide a   full copy of the notice and supporting basis   for the increase?
Tenant Interview Questions for the Intake File
Use these to complete the file before formal legal review:
- Did the tenant sign only   one fixed-term lease  , or were there later amendments?
- Does the lease contain any clause requiring the tenant to move out at the end of the term?
- Is the rental unit a   standard residential tenancy  , or could it fall into a special category:
- roommate/shared accommodation with owner
- co-op
- subsidized housing
- student housing
- employment-related housing
- What was the   monthly rent when the lease began  ?
- Has rent ever been increased before during this tenancy?
- On what date did the tenant   actually receive   the June 15, 2026 notice?
- Was the notice attached to the door, mailed, emailed, hand-delivered, or sent another way?
- Did the tenant ever agree in writing to a different rent amount or a new lease term?
- Has the landlord mentioned renovations, sale, personal occupancy, or redevelopment at any time?
- Has the tenant withheld rent, paid partial rent, or disputed the increase already?
- Are there language, disability, or access issues affecting the tenant’s ability to respond to notices?
- Has the tenant suffered any pressure tactics, threats, or statements like “pay the increase or leave”?
Practical Issue Flags to Spot Early
-   Possible invalid amount  : a   12% increase   may be problematic unless there is lawful authority for more than the permitted annual increase.
-   Possible notice problem  : notice dated   2026-06-15   for an increase starting   2026-08-01   may raise timing/service issues.
-   Lease-end confusion  : fixed-term tenancies in BC often require careful review of whether they continue or lawfully end.
-   Deposit compliance  : the   half-month security deposit   sounds facially ordinary, but confirm there was no excess deposit or unlawful extra charge.
-   No renovation basis in current facts  : that weakens any casual justification tied to major building work unless there is separate formal approval.
